Q006939:
## Model call versus agent
A plain model call (a chat completion or a single Responses API call) sends some input to a deployed model and gets a reply back. Nothing is saved in Foundry: every call has to carry its own system prompt and any tool settings, and the script in the stem sends only a prompt, so the model can only answer from what it learned in training.
An **agent** in Foundry Agent Service is a persisted definition that combines:
- a **model** from the Foundry model catalog,
- **instructions** that set its role, tone and rules,
- **tools** it may call, such as file search, code interpreter, web search, OpenAPI or function tools.
Foundry stores agents as **named, versioned assets**. Your app only names the agent; the same instructions and tools are applied to every request, and the model can decide to call a tool, read the result and then answer. (You can also pass instructions and tools in each Responses API call yourself; Learn calls that an ephemeral agent, because nothing is saved.)
## Example
A support bot defined as an agent always follows the support instructions and can search the product manuals with file search, instead of each app re-sending a long system prompt and having no access to the manuals.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Automatic fine-tuning:** creating an agent does not train or fine-tune anything. Instructions are sent to the model at run time and attached files are searched with tools, not used as training data.
- ✓ **B. Persisted model + instructions + tools (correct):** Learn describes an agent as a persisted definition that combines a model, instructions and tools and is stored as a named, versioned asset, which gives consistent behavior and lets the model use tools.
- ✗ **C. Larger context window:** an agent uses the context window of the model it is configured with; it does not split prompts across deployments or extend the model's limits.
- ✗ **D. Flat monthly price:** prompt agents are billed per call for model inference plus any tool usage, not with a flat per-agent rate.

## Key idea
An agent is a saved, versioned combination of model, instructions and tools; a plain model call is a single request that has none of these.
Q006940:
## The ways to build an agent in Foundry
Foundry Agent Service offers several paths, from least to most code:
- **Prompt agent**: defined entirely by configuration (model, instructions, tools). You can author it in the Foundry portal or with the SDK/REST API, and Foundry runs it. No application code, containers or compute to manage. Learn calls it the fastest path and suggests it for a first agent.
- **Voice-based prompt agent**: a prompt agent for real-time spoken conversations through Voice Live (preview).
- **Hosted agent**: your own code (Agent Framework, LangGraph and others) shipped as a container or a .zip; Foundry hosts it.
- **Ephemeral agent**: your app calls the Responses API directly and passes the instructions, model and tools in each call; nothing is saved in Foundry.
## Picking one
"No code, set it up and test it in the portal" points to a prompt agent: create it in the portal, chat with it in the agents playground, and call it from an app later if needed.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Voice-based prompt agent:** it is built for spoken, real-time conversations and is in preview; the HR team asked for a text assistant, not a voice experience.
- ✗ **B. Hosted agent:** hosted agents exist for teams that bring their own code and framework; the team would have to write, package and maintain that code.
- ✓ **C. Prompt agent (correct):** it is defined only by configuration in the portal or SDK, and Foundry runs it with no code, containers or compute for the team to maintain, exactly what the HR team asked for.
- ✗ **D. Ephemeral agent:** the definition lives in application code that the team would write and run; there is no saved agent to set up and test in the portal.

## Key idea
For a no-code agent that Foundry runs for you, create a prompt agent (model + instructions + tools) in the Foundry portal.
Q006941:
## What instructions do
Every prompt agent has **instructions**: the text that tells the model who it is, how to behave and what it must not do. They play the role of a system message, but they are saved as part of the agent definition, so:
- every conversation and every response uses them automatically,
- users never see or need to type them,
- changing them creates a new version of the agent that you can test and roll back.
## Writing good instructions
- State the role and audience: "You are a booking assistant for Contoso Tours."
- Set limits: "Only answer questions about Contoso tours. Politely decline other topics."
- Describe the tools and when to use them: "Use file search for tour details."
## Example
`instructions="You are a friendly assistant for Contoso Tours. Only discuss our tours and politely refuse other topics."`

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Agent instructions (correct):** instructions are part of the saved agent definition and steer the model on every response, so the tone and topic rules apply to all conversations without anyone repeating them.
- ✗ **B. First user message:** user messages are input, not configuration. Each new conversation would need the rules again, and a later user message could easily override them.
- ✗ **C. File search document:** file search retrieves passages that look relevant to a question to ground answers in facts; it is not a reliable place for behavior rules, which belong in the instructions.
- ✗ **D. Content filter settings:** content filters block harmful categories such as hate or violence; they cannot set a friendly tone or restrict the agent to a company's own topics.

## Key idea
Put an agent's role, tone and limits in its instructions; they are stored with the agent and applied to every response.
Q006942:
## Tool availability depends on two things
A tool in Foundry Agent Service can run only when **both** of these support it:
- the **model** the agent uses, and
- the **region** of the Foundry project (and of the model deployment).
Learn's troubleshooting guidance says: if either the region table or the model table shows "No", the tool can't run, even if the other shows "Yes". For example, code interpreter doesn't run in regions that show no for it, whatever model you choose.
## How to fix it
- Check the tool support by region and model tables on Learn.
- Confirm the model is really deployed in the project and region you are using.
- Use a different region or a model deployment that supports the tool.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Temperature setting:** temperature changes how varied the model's text is; it has nothing to do with whether a tool is supported in a region or by a model.
- ✗ **B. Uploaded CSV file:** code interpreter can run Python and do calculations without any uploaded file; files are optional input, not a prerequisite for enabling the tool.
- ✗ **C. Instructions naming the tool:** describing tools in the instructions helps the model choose when to call them, but it does not enable or disable a tool, and it would not cause an unsupported error.
- ✓ **D. Region support (correct):** the error appears when the region (or the actual deployment) does not support the tool, even though the model does; both must support it.

## Key idea
A Foundry agent tool runs only when both the model and the project's region support it; check both tables when you get a "tool not supported" error.
Q006943:
## Grounding an agent in your own documents
A model only knows what it learned in training. To make an agent answer from **your** documents, you give it a retrieval tool. In Foundry Agent Service the simplest one is **file search**:
1. Upload the files and add them to a **vector store** (the files are split into chunks and indexed by meaning).
2. Wait for ingestion to finish.
3. Attach file search with that vector store to the agent.
4. When a user asks something, the agent searches the store, gets the most relevant passages and answers from them.
This pattern is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). File search is GA; it has charges on top of the model's token fees. With the standard agent setup the files stay in your own storage and your Azure AI Search resource ingests them.
## Tip
In the instructions, tell the agent to use file search for product questions and to say when the manuals don't contain the answer.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Function calling:** the developer would have to build and run their own search over the manuals and return the results; file search already provides that retrieval without custom code.
- ✓ **B. File search (correct):** it indexes the uploaded manuals in a vector store and lets the agent retrieve the relevant passages for each question, so answers come from the company's private documents.
- ✗ **C. Code interpreter:** it runs Python in a sandbox for data analysis and charts. It is not a search index; reading 200 PDFs with code on every question would be slow and would not find the relevant passages by meaning.
- ✗ **D. Web search:** the manuals are not public, so a web search cannot return them, and answers would come from other websites instead of the company's own content.

## Key idea
To ground an agent in private documents, upload them to a vector store and attach the file search tool.
Q006944:
## Why models need a calculator
Large language models predict text; they are not reliable at exact arithmetic over many rows. **Code interpreter** solves this by letting the agent's model write Python, run it in a **sandboxed environment**, look at the result and try again if needed.
## What code interpreter can do
- Read uploaded files such as CSV or Excel.
- Calculate exact results (sums, growth rates, statistics).
- Produce files such as PNG charts that the app can download.
## Things to know
- It has charges beyond the model's token fees.
- Each conversation that uses it gets its own session; a session is active for up to one hour, with a 30-minute idle timeout.
- The sandbox is Microsoft-managed and isolated, so the generated code cannot touch your systems.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Web search:** the data is the manager's own CSV, so public web results would be irrelevant, and searching does not compute anything.
- ✗ **B. OpenAPI tool:** it would need an external charting service the company doesn't have, and it still would not compute the growth rates; code interpreter does both with no extra service.
- ✓ **C. Code interpreter (correct):** the model writes Python that computes the growth rates exactly and draws the chart, and the code runs in an isolated sandbox, so the arithmetic is done by code instead of guessed by the model.
- ✗ **D. File search:** retrieval returns passages of text that match a question; it does not perform calculations across all rows or produce charts.

## Key idea
Use code interpreter when an agent must calculate, analyze data files or generate charts; it runs model-written Python in a sandbox.
Q006945:
## How web search grounds an agent
The **web search** tool lets the agent's model retrieve current information from the public web before answering, and return the answer with inline citations. For a prompt agent you can add it directly, without creating a separate Bing resource or project connection.
## What compliance teams must know
Learn's important note on the tool says:
- Web search uses **Grounding with Bing Search** (and Bing Custom Search), which are governed by their own Grounding with Bing terms of use and the Microsoft Privacy Statement.
- The Microsoft Data Protection Addendum doesn't apply to data sent to these services, and **data transfers occur outside compliance and geographic boundaries**.
- Using them incurs costs.
Administrators can manage whether web search is allowed.
## Example
A user's question, possibly with personal details, is sent as a search query to Bing. Write instructions that keep personal data out of searches, or don't use web search for sensitive workloads.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Only uploaded pages:** that describes file search over a vector store. Web search queries the public web through Bing; it does not depend on files the startup uploads.
- ✗ **B. Hosted agents only:** Learn's quickstart adds web search directly to a prompt agent; hosted agents can use it too, but it is not limited to them.
- ✗ **C. No extra charge:** Learn states that using Grounding with Bing incurs costs; the search is not included in the model's token price.
- ✓ **D. Data leaves the boundary (correct):** web search relies on Grounding with Bing, governed by separate terms; the Data Protection Addendum doesn't apply and data can be transferred outside compliance and geographic boundaries.

## Key idea
Web search gives an agent current, cited web information through Grounding with Bing, but query data leaves your compliance boundary and incurs extra cost.
Q006946:
## How function calling works
A **function tool** describes a function to the model: its name, a description and its parameters (a JSON schema). The model never runs code. Instead:
1. The user asks "Where is order 1042?"
2. The model decides the function is needed and returns a **function call** item, for example `get_order_status` with `{"order_id": "1042"}`.
3. **Your application** runs the real function (here, a database lookup).
4. Your app sends the result back as a `function_call_output` item in the same conversation.
5. The agent uses the result to write the final answer.
This is client-side execution: the data and code stay in your app.
## Limits worth knowing
- Learn warns that runs expire 10 minutes after creation, so submit tool outputs in time.
- You add, remove or change function definitions with the SDK or REST API; the Foundry portal doesn't edit them, and Learn suggests testing function calling from code.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Client-side execution (correct):** with function calling the model only asks for the call with arguments; the developer's app executes it against the internal database and returns the output for the agent to use.
- ✗ **B. Model runs the code:** a model only generates text, including the structured request for a call; it cannot execute code or reach the retailer's database.
- ✗ **C. Managed sandbox:** that describes code interpreter, which runs model-written Python. Function tools are executed by your application, and the portal doesn't edit function definitions.
- ✗ **D. Web endpoint from a spec:** that is the OpenAPI tool, where Foundry calls an HTTP API described by a specification. A function tool is executed by the client application instead.

## Key idea
With a function tool, the model requests the call and your app executes it and returns the output; Foundry never runs your function.
Q006947:
## Two ways to let an agent call your systems
- **Function calling**: the model asks for a call and **your app** executes it. Good when the logic lives in the client.
- **OpenAPI tool**: you give the agent an **OpenAPI 3.0 or 3.1 specification**, and Foundry Agent Service calls the HTTP API **itself**. Good when an API already exists and the client should not run the calls.
## What the OpenAPI tool needs
- A specification in which each operation has an `operationId` (letters, `-` and `_`) and a clear description, so the model can choose the right operation.
- A **project connection**, even for anonymous APIs. Supported authentication: anonymous, API key, or the project's managed identity.
- Credentials stored in the connection, never in the specification, the prompt or source code.
## Example
An operation `getShipmentStatus` with a parameter `trackingNumber` lets the agent answer "Where is parcel 7781?" by calling the tracking API directly.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Function tool:** Foundry never executes function tools; the client app would have to run every call, which the company wants to avoid.
- ✓ **B. OpenAPI tool (correct):** it lets the agent call an existing HTTP API described by an OpenAPI 3.0/3.1 spec on the server side; each operation needs an operationId, and the tool uses a project connection for anonymous, key or managed identity authentication.
- ✗ **C. Code interpreter with key in instructions:** putting credentials in instructions is unsafe, and code interpreter runs in a sandbox for data analysis, not as a way to call company APIs.
- ✗ **D. File search:** indexing the specification only lets the agent quote it; file search cannot make HTTP requests to the API.

## Key idea
To have an agent call an existing REST API itself, use the OpenAPI tool with a spec that has operationIds and a project connection for authentication.
Q006948:
## Matching needs to tools
A prompt agent can use several tools at once; the model picks the right one for each part of a question. A quick guide to the GA built-in tools:
- **File search**: find and quote passages from your own documents (RAG over a vector store).
- **Code interpreter**: run Python in a sandbox for calculations, data files and charts.
- **Web search**: current public web information with citations.
- **OpenAPI tool**: call an existing HTTP API described by a specification.
- **Function calling**: ask your app to run one of its own functions.
## Example instructions
"Use file search for policy questions. Use code interpreter to calculate leave balances from the uploaded spreadsheet. Show the numbers you used."
Describing each tool in the instructions helps the model choose the right one.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. OpenAPI tool:** a specification describes HTTP operations of an API; policy documents are not API operations and gain nothing from being described that way.
- ✗ **B. Web search:** public labor-law pages are not the company's policy and add no calculation ability; it also sends queries outside the compliance boundary.
- ✓ **C. Code interpreter (correct):** exact balances come from running Python over the spreadsheet in a sandbox, which avoids the model guessing arithmetic.
- ✗ **D. Function calling:** the model never runs functions; the client app would have to execute them, and no such app logic is described here.
- ✓ **E. File search (correct):** the policy documents are private text, and file search retrieves the relevant passages so answers follow the company's own rules.

## Key idea
Combine tools by need: file search for answers from your documents, code interpreter for exact calculations on data files.
Q006949:
## Why an agent might ignore a tool
The model decides on each turn whether to call a tool. If the instructions never say what the tool is for, the model may answer from its own knowledge instead. Learn's troubleshooting checklist for "your agent doesn't call a tool":
- Confirm the tool is attached to the agent.
- Confirm the model supports the tool.
- Make the instructions specific: what each tool is for and when to use it, for example "For any product question, use file search and cite the guide."
- If you need deterministic behavior, set `tool_choice` to `required`.
- Review **traces** to see whether the model produced a tool call and what the tool returned.
## Testing in the agents playground
The agents playground lets you chat with the agent in the Foundry portal before writing an app. Change the instructions, save (which creates a new version), and test the same questions again.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Higher temperature:** temperature changes how varied the wording is; it is not a control for whether the model calls a tool and can make answers less reliable.
- ✗ **B. Recreate the agent:** tools added to an agent are part of its new version and are used; recreating it changes nothing about why the model skips the tool.
- ✗ **C. Switch to web search:** file search also returns answers grounded in, and citing, your files; web search would search the public web instead of the private product guides.
- ✓ **D. Clear instructions plus traces (correct):** telling the agent when to use file search is the main lever for tool use, and traces show whether the model called the tool and what it returned.

## Key idea
If an agent ignores a tool, tell it in the instructions when to use the tool, check traces, and use tool_choice required when you need a call every time.
Q006950:
## What a prompt agent is made of
A prompt agent is pure configuration: a **model**, **instructions** and optional **tools**. The model does the actual work; instructions and tools only steer it. So the one thing an agent cannot do without is a model it can call.
## Getting ready in the portal
1. Create a Foundry project.
2. Deploy a model from the model catalog (Learn's quickstart uses a `gpt-5-mini` deployment) and try it in the model playground.
3. In the **Build** section, select **Agents**, then **Create agent**, and give it a name; the agent uses your deployed model, and you add instructions.
4. Chat with it in the **agents playground**; follow-up questions show that it keeps the conversation history.
Tools are optional extras you add when a scenario needs them: file search needs a vector store, and some tools need a project connection. Learn also offers instant access models (preview) in some regions that skip the deployment step; exam answers stay on the generally available path of deploying a model first.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Deployed model (correct):** an agent is a model plus instructions and tools, and Learn lists a model deployed in the project as the prerequisite; without one the agent has nothing to generate replies with.
- ✗ **B. Container image:** containers are for hosted agents that run your own code; Foundry runs prompt agents for you with no code or containers.
- ✗ **C. Vector store:** a vector store is needed only when you add the file search tool; a prompt agent with no tools answers from the model and its instructions.
- ✗ **D. Bing resource and connection:** web search is an optional tool, and Learn adds it to a prompt agent without a separate Bing resource or connection; general questions need no web access.

## Key idea
Deploy a model first; a prompt agent is that model plus instructions and optional tools, tested in the agents playground.
Q006951:
## Agents are versioned assets
In the current Foundry Agent Service, an agent is stored as a **named, versioned asset**:
- Creating or changing the agent (for example with `project.agents.create_version(...)` in the SDK, or saving in the portal) produces a **new version**.
- Agents are identified by **name and version**; they no longer have a GUID "agent ID".
- You can roll back to any previous version or compare versions.
- Publishing promotes the agent to a managed resource with a stable endpoint that apps can call.
## Why this matters
Versioning lets you try new instructions, model choices or tools in the agents playground, compare results, and go back if quality drops, instead of retyping old settings.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Name plus version (correct):** every saved change is snapshotted as a new version of the same named agent, so she can roll back or compare with the earlier instructions.
- ✗ **B. Overwrite in place:** Foundry keeps earlier versions automatically; she does not need to remember or retype the old definition.
- ✗ **C. Session-only changes:** saving persists the definition in the project as a version; no export is needed to keep it.
- ✗ **D. New GUID per save:** agents in the current service are identified by name and version, not by a GUID agent ID, and a change does not create a separate agent.

## Key idea
Foundry agents are named, versioned assets: each change makes a new version you can compare with or roll back to.
Q006952:
## Connecting a client to an agent
A client app for a Foundry agent uses the **Azure AI Projects** SDK (`azure-ai-projects` for Python, version 2.x for the current agents). It needs:
- the **project endpoint**, shown on the project's overview page in the Foundry portal, in the form `https://<resource-name>.services.ai.azure.com/api/projects/<project-name>`;
- a **credential** (Microsoft Entra ID, for example `DefaultAzureCredential()`);
- the **agent name** (agents are identified by name and version).
## Example
```
project = AIProjectClient(endpoint=PROJECT_ENDPOINT, credential=DefaultAzureCredential())
openai = project.get_openai_client(agent_name="support-bot")
```
The second line returns a client that is bound to that agent, ready to create conversations and responses.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Subscription and resource group:** these identify Azure resources for management, but the SDK connects to the project endpoint URL, not to a URL built from them.
- ✗ **B. Portal URL and email address:** ai.azure.com is the portal, not an API endpoint, and agents are not selected by their owner's email address.
- ✓ **C. Project endpoint and agent name (correct):** the project client connects to the project endpoint with an Entra ID credential, and the agent name selects which agent's instructions and tools are used.
- ✗ **D. Deployment API key and model name:** the agent already has its model configured; the client names the agent, and Learn's samples sign in with Entra ID rather than a deployment key.

## Key idea
An agent client needs the Foundry project endpoint, an Entra ID credential and the agent's name.
Q006953:
## Entra ID authentication and roles
The agent samples on Learn authenticate with **Microsoft Entra ID** through `DefaultAzureCredential` from `azure-identity`. On a developer machine it picks up the account you signed in with using `az login`; in Azure it can use a managed identity.
Signing in proves **who** you are. Azure RBAC then decides **what** you may do. Each person or identity needs a role on the Foundry project:
- **Foundry User** (previously named Azure AI User): build and develop in projects, including creating and running agents. It is the role Learn lists as the prerequisite for agent work.
- **Foundry Agent Consumer**: least-privilege role for identities that only call agents.
- Do **not** use **Azure AI Developer** for Foundry projects: Learn notes it is scoped to Azure Machine Learning workspaces and Foundry hubs, not to Foundry projects.
## Example
Learn notes that Foundry User is assigned automatically to a user who can assign roles when they create the project in the portal, which is how the developer got it. Her colleague has no role yet, so his token is valid but his call is refused.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Stored username and password:** embedding credentials in code is insecure and would make every call run as the developer; the fix is to give the colleague a role.
- ✓ **B. Foundry User role (correct):** the colleague's sign-in works, but he has no role on the project; Foundry User (formerly Azure AI User) is the role Learn lists for creating and running agents.
- ✗ **C. Email in instructions:** instructions steer the model's answers; they play no part in authentication or authorization.
- ✗ **D. Azure AI Developer:** Learn warns not to use this role for Foundry work because it applies to Azure Machine Learning workspaces and hubs, not to Foundry projects.

## Key idea
Entra ID sign-in identifies the caller; the caller also needs an RBAC role such as Foundry User on the project to use agents.
Q006954:
## Keyless authentication with Microsoft Entra ID
Microsoft recommends **Microsoft Entra ID** authentication for Foundry because it gives fine-grained RBAC; a key instead grants full access without role restrictions.
`DefaultAzureCredential` (from `azure-identity`) tries several sources in order, so the same code works everywhere:
- On a developer laptop: the account signed in with `az login` (or Visual Studio Code).
- In Azure (App Service, Functions, VMs, containers): a **managed identity**, whose credentials Azure handles automatically.
The identity still needs an RBAC role on the Foundry project, such as Foundry User (formerly Azure AI User) or the least-privilege Foundry Agent Consumer for callers that only use agents.
## Example
```
project = AIProjectClient(endpoint=PROJECT_ENDPOINT, credential=DefaultAzureCredential())
```
No secret appears in code or settings; locally it uses `az login`, in App Service it uses the managed identity.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Hard-coded client secret:** a client secret in the script is exactly the kind of credential in code that the rule bans.
- ✗ **B. Resource key in app settings:** a key is a secret in configuration, which the rule forbids, and it grants full access without RBAC restrictions.
- ✗ **C. Pasted bearer token:** access tokens expire after a short time and pasting them into code is both a secret in code and unworkable to maintain.
- ✓ **D. Managed identity with a role (correct):** in App Service a managed identity gets tokens automatically, and a Foundry role on the project authorizes it, with no secret to store.
- ✓ **E. DefaultAzureCredential with az login (correct):** locally it uses the developer's signed-in Entra ID account, so no key or password is stored anywhere.

## Key idea
For keyless agent clients, use DefaultAzureCredential: az login on developer machines and a managed identity with a Foundry role in Azure.
Q006955:
## Conversations hold the history
In Foundry Agent Service, three runtime pieces work together:
- **Agent**: reusable model, instructions and tools.
- **Conversation**: persisted input and output items, so later turns have server-side history.
- **Response**: one unit of execution that runs the agent against the input (and the conversation) and appends output items.
A follow-up question works only when it is sent to the **same conversation** as the earlier turns.
## Example
```
conversation = openai.conversations.create()
r1 = openai.responses.create(conversation=conversation.id, input="What is the size of France?")
r2 = openai.responses.create(conversation=conversation.id, input="And what is the capital?")
```
The second call can answer "And what is the capital?" because the conversation already contains the question about France. Creating a new conversation for every message starts with an empty history each time.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Reuse one conversation (correct):** a conversation persists the items of earlier turns, so sending every message of a session to the same conversation ID gives the agent the context it needs.
- ✗ **B. create_version per message:** that only saves a new version of the agent definition; agents don't store chat history, conversations do.
- ✗ **C. History in instructions:** instructions are the agent's shared configuration for all users; editing them per turn would mix users' chats and create endless versions.
- ✗ **D. More quota:** quota limits throughput; a brand-new conversation is empty no matter how many tokens are allowed.

## Key idea
Create a conversation once per chat session and pass its ID on every response; a new conversation means a new, empty history.
Q006956:
## The client flow for an agent
With the current Azure AI Projects SDK (2.x) a lightweight agent client does four things:
1. Connect: `project = AIProjectClient(endpoint=..., credential=DefaultAzureCredential())`.
2. Get a client bound to the agent: `openai = project.get_openai_client(agent_name="tour-guide")`.
3. Start a conversation: `conversation = openai.conversations.create()`.
4. Send each message and run the agent in one call: `response = openai.responses.create(conversation=conversation.id, input="...")`, then read `response.output_text`.
## Compared with the classic API
The classic Agents API (deprecated, retiring March 31, 2027) used a **thread**, added a **message**, started a **run** and polled its status. In the current service the conversation replaces the thread, and a single **response** both sends the input and runs the agent.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. conversations.create:** this creates an empty conversation to hold history; it does not run the agent or produce a reply.
- ✗ **B. agents.create_version:** this saves a new version of the agent definition (model, instructions, tools); it is an authoring call, not a way to ask a question.
- ✓ **C. responses.create with the conversation (correct):** a response runs the agent against the new input and the conversation's history, and `output_text` holds the agent's reply.
- ✗ **D. models.list:** this lists models; it doesn't take a conversation or input and never runs the agent.

## Key idea
To chat with an agent, create a conversation once and call responses.create with the conversation ID and the user's input; read output_text.
Q006957:
## Classic agents versus current agents
The **classic** Foundry Agent Service (Agents API v1, Azure AI Projects 1.x) used:
- **Thread**: a conversation session that stored messages.
- **Message**: a user or agent entry in the thread.
- **Run**: invoking the agent on the thread; the app polled its status (`queued`, `in_progress`, `requires_action`, `completed`).
Learn marks agents (classic) as deprecated, to be retired on **March 31, 2027**, and points to the generally available new Foundry Agent Service.
## The current model
The current service (Azure AI Projects 2.x) uses three components:
- **Agent**: named, versioned definition (model, instructions, tools).
- **Conversation**: persisted history items, the successor to the thread.
- **Response**: one call that takes the input, runs the agent against the conversation and returns the output items.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Project connection:** connections store how to reach external resources such as an OpenAPI service; they have nothing to do with conversation history.
- ✓ **B. Conversation and response (correct):** conversations persist the history across turns like threads did, and a response combines adding the input and running the agent in a single call.
- ✗ **C. Agent version:** versions snapshot the agent's definition; user messages are never stored as instructions or new versions.
- ✗ **D. Vector store:** a vector store holds indexed files for the file search tool; it does not keep chat history, and messages are not uploaded as files.

## Key idea
In the current Foundry Agent Service, conversations replace threads and a single response replaces adding a message plus starting and polling a run.
Q006958:
## One agent, many conversations
An agent definition is shared: everyone who calls it gets the same model, instructions and tools. Chat history is not part of the agent; it lives in **conversations**.
Good practice (from Learn's guidance on threads, which conversations replaced):
- Give **each user their own conversation(s)** to keep their histories isolated.
- Start a **new conversation** for a new topic or when a user wants to "start over".
- Very long conversations can increase latency, so long-running chats may also be split.
- Conversations are stored data: plan retention and deletion for privacy and compliance.
## Example
The web app stores the conversation ID in each student's session. "New chat" creates another conversation; the next question goes to that ID.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. One shared conversation:** the agent would see every student's messages as context and could reveal or mix them in answers; filtering only in the page does not protect the model's context.
- ✗ **B. Daily shared conversation:** students would still share history during the day, which breaks isolation, and a scheduled delete does not let a student start fresh.
- ✗ **C. Version per student:** versions snapshot the agent definition, not chat history; creating hundreds of versions would not isolate conversations.
- ✓ **D. Per-student conversations (correct):** each conversation keeps only that student's items, so histories stay isolated, and a new conversation gives a clean start for a fresh topic.

## Key idea
Share one agent but give each user (and each new topic) its own conversation to keep history isolated.
Q006959:
## The function calling loop in a client
With function tools, the conversation pauses until **your app** supplies the result:
1. Your app sends the user's input with `responses.create(...)`.
2. The model decides it needs `get_weather` and the response contains a **function call** item with the arguments (for example `{"city": "Seoul"}`), not final text.
3. Your app runs its own `get_weather` function.
4. Your app sends a follow-up request containing a `function_call_output` item with the result, in the **same conversation**.
5. The agent uses the result and returns the final answer in `output_text`.
## Common mistakes
- Only reading `output_text` and ignoring function call items.
- Asking the same question again, which just produces another function call.
- Waiting too long: Learn warns that runs expire 10 minutes after creation, so submit tool outputs promptly.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Ask again and wait:** Foundry never executes function tools, so repeating the question only produces another function call request.
- ✗ **B. New conversation:** the call does not end the conversation, and a new conversation would lose the pending function call and the context it belongs to.
- ✗ **C. Remove the tool:** a function_call item is the normal, successful step of function calling, not a failure; removing the tool would lose the weather capability.
- ✓ **D. Return the function output (correct):** the model asked the client to run get_weather; after the app runs it and sends a function_call_output item in the same conversation, the agent can produce the final text answer.

## Key idea
When a response contains a function call, run the function in your app and send a function_call_output in the same conversation to get the final answer.
Q006960:
## Agents, conversations and responses
Learn describes three runtime components that work together:
- **Agent**: a reusable definition (model, instructions, tools). Use it when many requests need the same behavior.
- **Conversation**: a durable object that stores **items**: user and assistant messages, tool calls, tool outputs and other data. Use it when later turns need server-side history.
- **Response**: one unit of execution. It runs a model or an agent against the input (and the conversation, if one is given) and produces output items, including the text in `output_text`.
## How they fit together
A support app picks an agent, creates a conversation for the customer, and sends each question as a response in that conversation; the response's output is appended to the same conversation, so the next question is answered in context.
A response doesn't need an agent: you can call a model directly and pass everything in the request. Without a conversation, an app can still chain turns by referencing a previous stored response (`previous_response_id`).
## What is not true
The agent definition never stores chat history; it is shared configuration. History lives in conversations or stored responses.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Conversation persists history (correct):** Learn describes a conversation as the component that supplies persisted input and output items to responses, so later turns have server-side history.
- ✗ **B. Agent required:** Learn shows responses created directly against a model with no agent, which is the plain model call of a chat client.
- ✗ **C. Responses written into the agent:** agents hold only the reusable definition; chat history is never written into it or shared across users.
- ✗ **D. Text messages only:** conversations store items, including tool calls and tool outputs, so the next turn can reuse that context.
- ✓ **E. Response as execution (correct):** Learn defines a response as running a model or agent against input and producing output items; every interaction is one response.

## Key idea
An agent is the reusable definition, a conversation holds the history items, and a response is one run that produces output.
Q006961:
## Speech to text comes in three shapes
Speech recognition (speech to text) turns spoken audio into written text. Azure Speech in Foundry Tools offers it in three ways, and the right one depends on **when** you need the text and **how much** audio you have:
- **Real-time transcription**: audio is streamed (for example from a microphone) and text, including intermediate results, comes back as the person speaks. Used for live captions and agent assist.
- **Fast transcription**: a pre-recorded file is sent and the transcript comes back synchronously, faster than real time. Used for a voicemail or a single meeting recording you need right away.
- **Batch transcription**: large numbers of stored audio files are processed **asynchronously**; you submit a job and collect the transcripts later. Learn names call-center recordings and large volumes of captions as typical uses.
## Example
A call center that records 5,000 calls a day submits one batch job each evening; by morning every call has a transcript that can be searched or passed to text analysis for sentiment.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Text to speech:** this is speech synthesis, the reverse direction (text in, audio out); it cannot produce a searchable transcript from recorded audio.
- ✓ **B. Batch transcription (correct):** the calls are already stored, the volume is large and the results are only needed the next morning, which is exactly the asynchronous, high-volume case batch transcription is designed for.
- ✗ **C. Pronunciation assessment:** it evaluates accuracy and fluency for language learners and does not deliver the call transcripts the analysts need to search.
- ✗ **D. Real-time transcription:** it is built for live streams where text is needed while people talk; nothing here is live, so streaming thousands of stored files would add effort and cost with no benefit.

## Key idea
For large volumes of stored audio where results can wait, use batch transcription; use real-time transcription only when text is needed while people speak.
Q006962:
## Speech synthesis
**Text to speech**, also called **speech synthesis**, converts written text into spoken audio. It is the reverse of speech recognition (speech to text). Azure Speech in Foundry Tools provides:
- **Standard voices**: highly natural, out-of-the-box **neural voices** in many languages and locales. Learn lists turning e-books into audiobooks, chatbot and voice-assistant replies and in-car navigation as typical uses.
- **Custom voice**: a unique voice for a brand, trained from recordings of a voice talent (a Limited Access feature you must apply for).
- **Batch synthesis** for long audio such as audiobooks and lectures, where the result does not have to come back instantly.
## Direction matters
A quick way to classify a speech scenario: if the input is **audio** and the output is **text**, it is speech recognition; if the input is **text** and the output is **audio**, it is speech synthesis.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Language identification:** it only tells you which language is spoken in audio; it produces no narration and would still leave the company hiring narrators.
- ✗ **B. Speech translation:** it translates **spoken** audio into another language; the company has written text in one language and simply wants it read aloud.
- ✓ **C. Text to speech (correct):** the input is existing written text and the desired output is natural spoken audio, which is exactly what speech synthesis with neural voices provides, with no recording session needed.
- ✗ **D. Speech to text:** it goes the other way (audio in, text out) and would still need someone to record every module, which is the work the company wants to avoid.

## Key idea
Text in and audio out is speech synthesis (text to speech); audio in and text out is speech recognition (speech to text).
Q006963:
## Controlling how a voice speaks
Plain text sent to text to speech is spoken with default settings. **Speech Synthesis Markup Language (SSML)** is an XML-based markup you send instead of plain text to fine-tune the output. With SSML you can:
- change the **speaking rate**, **pitch** and **volume**;
- add **pauses** (breaks) between phrases;
- improve **pronunciation**, including your own lexicon for unusual words;
- switch speaking styles or use several voices in one document.
## Recognition tools are a different side
Custom speech and phrase lists improve **speech recognition** (speech to text): they help the service understand words people say. They have no effect on how a synthesized voice sounds.
## Example
A small SSML document wraps the warning in a slower `prosody` rate, adds a `break` before "turn left" and gives the street name a custom pronunciation, while keeping the same voice name.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Custom speech model:** custom speech improves speech **recognition** accuracy for domain words; the app's problem is how its synthesized voice speaks, not how it hears drivers.
- ✗ **B. Language identification:** it detects the spoken language of incoming audio; it cannot fix a mispronounced word, the reading speed or missing pauses.
- ✓ **C. SSML (correct):** it is the markup for tuning text to speech output, and pronunciation, speaking rate and pauses are exactly the controls it provides while the voice stays the same.
- ✗ **D. Phrase list:** phrase lists also boost **recognition** of expected words in incoming audio and do nothing to the pronunciation or pacing of synthesized speech.

## Key idea
To change how a text to speech voice pronounces, paces or pauses, use SSML; custom speech and phrase lists only improve recognition.
Q006964:
## Base model versus custom speech
Out of the box, speech recognition uses a **base model** trained by Microsoft on commonly used spoken language. It works well in most scenarios, but Learn notes it may not be enough when audio contains **industry jargon** or difficult acoustic conditions.
**Custom speech** lets you augment the base model:
- **Text data** (related sentences, terms) improves recognition of domain-specific vocabulary.
- **Audio with reference (human) transcripts** improves recognition for specific audio conditions such as background noise.
- You test with the **word error rate (WER)**: compare the base model's transcript with a human transcript; a high WER suggests training a custom model.
A custom model is deployed to a custom endpoint (batch transcription can use it without one) and can serve real-time speech to text, speech translation and batch transcription.
## Example
A hospital uploads drug formularies and dictations with corrected transcripts, trains a model, sees WER fall on its test set and deploys it for dictation.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Custom speech model (correct):** training on domain text and transcribed audio is how custom speech improves recognition of jargon, and WER gives an objective comparison with the base model.
- ✗ **B. Same-language speech translation:** translation converts speech into another language; it does not teach the recognizer new vocabulary, so misrecognized terms stay wrong.
- ✗ **C. Different neural voice:** neural voices are text to speech output; switching voices has no effect on how speech to text understands what doctors say.
- ✗ **D. SSML with a custom lexicon:** SSML shapes **synthesized** speech; it changes how a voice reads text aloud, not how dictated audio is recognized.

## Key idea
When speech to text misses domain vocabulary, train a custom speech model with domain text and transcribed audio and measure it with word error rate.
Q006965:
## Speech translation
**Speech translation** combines recognition and translation: it takes spoken audio in a source language and returns **translated text**, **synthesized translated speech**, or both, in real time. Learn describes it as real-time, multi-language **speech-to-speech** and **speech-to-text** translation.
- The standard API translates from a specified source language into target languages.
- **Live Interpreter** goes further for conversations: it identifies the spoken language continuously without being told, handles language switching in one session and speaks the translation in a natural voice.
## How it differs from nearby features
- Speech to text keeps the same language; it only writes down what was said.
- Diarization labels **who** spoke; it does not change the language.
- Custom voice changes **how** synthesized speech sounds; it does not translate.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Custom voice:** a branded voice improves how announcements sound, but it performs no recognition or translation of what the passenger says.
- ✓ **B. Speech translation (correct):** the requirement is live, spoken input in one language turned into spoken output in another, which is the speech-to-speech translation capability.
- ✗ **C. Speech to text with diarization:** diarization separates speakers in a transcript; the text stays in the original language, so neither side understands the other.
- ✗ **D. Batch transcription:** it works asynchronously on stored recordings after the fact and produces same-language text, so the passenger would never hear a reply during the conversation.

## Key idea
Live spoken input in one language to text or speech in another is speech translation; speech to text and diarization never change the language.
Q006966:
## Recognition versus synthesis
- **Speech recognition (speech to text)**: audio in, text out. Examples: captions, dictation, transcribing calls or voicemail, and the recognition step behind voice commands.
- **Speech synthesis (text to speech)**: text in, audio out. Examples: audiobooks, spoken replies from a chatbot or voice assistant, in-car navigation prompts, reading teaching materials aloud.
Learn lists converting e-books into audiobooks and enhancing in-car navigation systems as neural voice scenarios.
## Pronunciation assessment
Pronunciation assessment listens to a learner and scores accuracy and fluency. It analyses **incoming** speech, so it belongs with recognition, not synthesis.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Pronunciation scoring:** the learner's spoken audio is analysed and scored, so the service is listening (recognition), not speaking.
- ✗ **B. Voicemail to text:** a recorded voice message becomes written text, which is speech recognition (transcription).
- ✗ **C. Live captions:** the presenter's audio becomes on-screen text, which is real-time speech recognition.
- ✓ **D. Audiobook narration (correct):** the e-book is text and the commuter hears audio, so the feature is text to speech.
- ✓ **E. Spoken directions (correct):** the navigation system has the directions as text and speaks them to the driver, which is speech synthesis.

## Key idea
If the app produces audio from text it is speech synthesis; if it turns spoken audio into text or scores it, it is speech recognition.
Q006967:
## What makes a voice sound natural
Human speech is not just the right sounds: it has **prosody**, the rhythm, stress and intonation that change with meaning. Older synthesis approaches often sounded flat because they struggled with prosody.
Azure Speech's **standard voices** are **neural voices**: deep neural networks predict prosody and synthesize the voice **at the same time**, which Learn says gives more fluid and natural-sounding output and reduces listening fatigue.
## Related terms
- **Standard voice**: an out-of-the-box neural voice (called Neural on the pricing page).
- **HD voices**: higher-quality voices for more versatile scenarios.
- **Custom voice**: a neural voice trained for one brand from a voice talent's recordings (Limited Access).
- **SSML**: markup to adjust pitch, rate, pauses and pronunciation of any of these voices.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Deep neural networks predicting prosody (correct):** neural voices model stress and intonation together with the audio itself, which is why they sound close to a human speaker.
- ✗ **B. Playing back word recordings:** stitching stored recordings together describes older concatenative ideas and could never cover every word or sentence naturally.
- ✗ **C. Sentiment analysis choosing recordings:** sentiment analysis is a text analysis technique; neural synthesis generates audio rather than picking prerecorded clips by mood.
- ✗ **D. Phonetic text at a fixed pitch:** a fixed pitch and pace is exactly the flat, robotic delivery neural voices avoid by predicting prosody.

## Key idea
Neural text to speech uses deep neural networks to predict prosody and voice together, which makes synthesized speech sound humanlike.
Q006968:
## Who said what
A plain transcript is one long stream of text. **Diarization** is the speech to text feature that distinguishes and separates the **different speakers** in a recording and tags the text with a speaker label, for example `Guest-1` and `Guest-2`. Learn notes it is particularly useful for conversations, meetings and any multi-speaker audio.
## Other recognition helpers
- **Language identification** detects which language is being spoken.
- **Phrase lists** give the recognizer words that are likely to appear (names, product terms) to improve accuracy.
- **Custom speech** trains a model for domain vocabulary or acoustic conditions.
None of these tells you which person spoke.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Custom voice:** it is a text to speech feature for creating synthetic voices and does nothing to label speakers in a transcript.
- ✗ **B. Language identification:** it identifies **languages**, not people; two participants speaking English would get the same label.
- ✓ **C. Diarization (correct):** separating and labelling individual speakers in single-channel audio is exactly what diarization does.
- ✗ **D. Phrase list:** it improves recognition of expected words such as names, but the transcript still would not say who spoke each sentence.

## Key idea
To label who said what in a transcript, use diarization; phrase lists and language identification improve accuracy or detect language only.
Q006969:
## Standard voices versus custom voice
- **Standard voices** are neural voices anyone with a resource can use straight away.
- **Custom voice** (professional voice fine-tuning and personal voice) creates a voice unique to a brand or product from a set of **audio recordings and matching transcripts** of a voice talent.
## Why it is restricted
A realistic synthetic copy of a real person's voice can be misused, for example for impersonation. So Microsoft makes custom voice a **Limited Access** feature: you apply, describe your use case and wait for approval. Responsible-use guidance asks for the **voice talent's consent** and for disclosure that a voice is synthetic.
## Example
A bank applies for access, signs a consent agreement with its voice actor, uploads studio recordings with transcripts and gets a voice that only its own applications can use.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Custom speech model first:** custom speech improves **recognition** and is a separate feature; synthesis voices are not built from a recognizer.
- ✓ **B. Limited Access with talent consent (correct):** Learn describes custom voice as having limited access for responsible use, and voice talent must agree to the creation of a synthetic version of their voice.
- ✗ **C. Open to all, clone any voice:** custom voice is not open by default, and cloning a public figure from a video without consent is exactly the misuse the restrictions exist to prevent.
- ✗ **D. No audio needed:** custom voice is trained from recordings of the voice talent with transcripts; a written personality description cannot produce a specific person's voice.

## Key idea
Custom voice is a Limited Access feature: apply for approval, record a consenting voice talent, and disclose synthetic speech responsibly.
Q006970:
## Matching the transcription mode to the timing
Azure Speech in Foundry Tools offers three ways to run speech to text:
- **Real-time**: audio is streamed and text arrives as it is recognized, including **intermediate (partial) results** that are refined. Learn lists real-time transcription for accessibility, and its captioning scenario relies on these partial results.
- **Fast transcription**: a recorded **file** goes in and the transcript returns synchronously, faster than real time. Good for a voicemail or a meeting recording you need soon after it ends.
- **Batch**: many stored files processed asynchronously; results come later.
## Example
Live captions in a meeting tool must keep up with the speaker, so they use real-time recognition; the same tool may later run batch transcription to produce a searchable archive.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Hourly fast transcription:** even though each file returns quickly, waiting for an hour of audio before transcribing makes the captions far too late for a live audience.
- ✗ **B. Text to speech with SSML:** that produces audio from text; captions need the reverse, text from the presenter's audio.
- ✗ **C. Batch transcription:** it only starts after the recording exists, so viewers would see nothing during the webinar.
- ✓ **D. Real-time transcription (correct):** captions during a live talk need text while the speaker is still talking, and intermediate results keep the delay low.

## Key idea
Live captions need real-time transcription; fast transcription suits single recorded files and batch suits large stored volumes.
Q006971:
## Three classic vision techniques
- **Image classification**: the model looks at the whole image and predicts **one label** for it ("apple"). Learn's example is a checkout scale that identifies a single type of produce.
- **Object detection**: the model examines regions of the image and returns **each object found**, with a label and the **coordinates of a bounding box**. This works when several items appear in one image.
- **Semantic segmentation**: the model classifies **individual pixels** by the object they belong to, giving a much more precise outline than a box.
## Example
A photo with a banana, a milk carton and a loaf of bread produces three detections, each with a confidence score and a rectangle, so the checkout can count and price each item.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Object detection (correct):** several items in one image, each needing a label and a location, is the textbook case for object detection with bounding boxes.
- ✗ **B. Image classification:** one label per image fits a single item on a scale, but it cannot list several items or say where each one is.
- ✗ **C. Image captioning:** a caption is one general sentence about the scene and does not give a structured label and location for each item.
- ✗ **D. Optical character recognition:** OCR extracts text; produce often has no printed label, and reading text does not locate each item.

## Key idea
One label for the whole image is classification; several labelled objects with bounding boxes is object detection; pixel-level outlines are segmentation.
Q006972:
## From labels to pixels
Computer vision techniques differ in how precisely they locate things:
- **Image classification**: one label for the whole image, no location.
- **Object detection**: a label plus a **rectangular bounding box** for each object.
- **Semantic segmentation**: a class for **every pixel**. Learn describes it as a more sophisticated way to detect objects that gives a much more precise prediction of where they are.
Because segmentation follows the true outline, you can count the pixels of a class and convert them to an area, something a rectangle cannot do for irregular shapes.
## Example
An aerial photo where flood water spreads along a winding river: a bounding box around the water also covers dry streets and fields, while a segmentation mask marks only the water pixels.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Object detection:** boxes are rectangles, so for winding flood water they include lots of dry land and overstate the area.
- ✗ **B. Image tagging:** tags describe what appears in the image but give neither location nor area.
- ✗ **C. Image classification:** a flooded or dry label per photo gives no location or area at all within the photo.
- ✓ **D. Semantic segmentation (correct):** pixel-level classification follows irregular outlines, so the agency can measure the flooded area precisely.

## Key idea
When you need exact shapes or areas, use semantic segmentation; bounding boxes from object detection are only rectangles.
Q006973:
## Describing an image with words
Modern multimodal vision models learn the relationships between visual features and language, so they can **describe** images:
- **Captioning** produces a sentence in natural language, for example "A person eating an apple in a park." Ideal for alt text and accessibility.
- **Tagging** returns a list of keywords, from thousands of recognizable objects, living things, scenery and actions (for example `outdoor`, `tree`, `person`, `eating`). Ideal for search and filtering.
Learn's digital asset management example combines exactly these: automatically generating captions for images and attaching keywords so they're searchable.
In Azure, the Image Analysis API of Azure Vision in Foundry Tools offers captions and tags today, but it is deprecated and retires on September 25, 2028; Learn points new solutions to multimodal models in Microsoft Foundry or Azure Content Understanding in Foundry Tools. The concepts stay the same.
## What the other techniques return
- OCR returns **text that is written in the image**, not a description.
- Segmentation returns a **pixel mask**, useful for measuring or editing, not for search.
- Face identification matches people against a known group and is a Limited Access feature.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Face identification:** it matches people to a stored group, which is not the requirement, and Microsoft restricts it as a Limited Access feature.
- ✗ **B. Optical character recognition:** it only reads text that appears in the image; most news photos describe scenes rather than contain text.
- ✓ **C. Image tagging (correct):** keywords for objects, scenery and actions give editors the searchable metadata they asked for.
- ✗ **D. Semantic segmentation:** a pixel mask gives no sentence and no searchable keywords.
- ✓ **E. Image captioning (correct):** a complete sentence describing the photo is exactly what screen-reader alt text needs.

## Key idea
Captioning gives a descriptive sentence and tagging gives searchable keywords; OCR only reads text that is visible in the image.
Q006974:
## Optical character recognition (OCR)
**OCR**, also called text recognition or text extraction, uses machine learning to read **printed or handwritten text** from images. Learn lists posters, **street signs** and product labels, as well as documents like articles, forms and invoices. The text comes back as words, lines and paragraphs, with their positions in the image.
## Where OCR is used
- General photos of signs, labels and whiteboards (image OCR).
- Text-heavy scanned or digital documents (document reading, often the first step of document field extraction).
## Example
A photo of a no-parking sign returns the lines `NO PARKING` and `MON-FRI 8AM-6PM`; the app then sends the text to a translation service.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Image tagging:** tags describe what is in the image (a sign, a pole) but not what the sign says.
- ✓ **B. Optical character recognition (correct):** the app needs the actual words written on the signs and notices, printed or handwritten, which is exactly what OCR extracts.
- ✗ **C. Object detection:** it locates the sign with a box and a label, but it does not read the text on it.
- ✗ **D. Image captioning:** a caption summarizes the scene in general words and does not transcribe the notice's actual text.

## Key idea
To get the words written in an image, printed or handwritten, use OCR; tags, detection and captions only describe what is visible.
Q006975:
## Why face features are restricted
Facial recognition can affect privacy and civil liberties, so Microsoft limits it under its Responsible AI principles.
- **Face detection** (finding faces and returning their location) is available **without registration**. It is the first step for every other face operation, and is also useful for things like blurring faces for privacy.
- **Face identification** (one-to-many: who is this, from a known group) and **face verification** (one-to-one: are these two faces the same person) are **Limited Access**. Customers must register through an intake form, select an approved use case, and access is limited to **customers managed by Microsoft**. These features are not supported on the Free (F0) tier.
- Since June 2020, use of Azure facial recognition **by or for U.S. police departments is prohibited**.
## Retired attributes
Microsoft **retired** facial analysis that infers **emotion** and **gender**, and limited others (age, smile, facial hair, hair, makeup), because they can lead to stereotyping or unfair treatment.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. U.S. police after registration:** use by or for U.S. police departments is prohibited outright; registration does not change that.
- ✓ **B. Detection without registration (correct):** Learn states that the Face Detection operation is available without registration.
- ✗ **C. Emotion recognition after registration:** emotion inference was retired, so no registration unlocks it.
- ✗ **D. Free tier for anyone:** identification and verification need approval and are not supported on the Free (F0) tier at all.
- ✓ **E. Identification and verification are registered and limited (correct):** these are Limited Access features that require a registration form and are offered only to customers and partners managed by Microsoft.

## Key idea
Face detection is open, identification and verification are Limited Access for approved Microsoft-managed customers, and emotion and gender inference are retired.
Q006976:
## Face analysis that Microsoft retired
Face detection can optionally return attributes such as head pose or whether a person wears glasses. These are **general predictions, not actual classifications**.
Microsoft reviewed attributes that try to infer **emotional states** and **identity attributes**, because if misused they can subject people to stereotyping, discrimination or unfair denial of services. The result:
- **Retired**: emotion and gender.
- **Limited**: age, smile, facial hair, hair and makeup (contact the Face team with a responsible use case).
## Responsible AI link
This is a concrete example of the fairness and privacy principles shaping a product: some capabilities are removed rather than merely gated.
## Example
A team that wants audience insight can instead count people entering (people detection) or run anonymous surveys, without inferring sensitive traits from faces.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Retired capabilities (correct):** emotion and gender inference were retired from the Face service, so the proposal cannot be built with it, whatever the tier or registration.
- ✗ **B. Enterprise tier only:** tier has nothing to do with it; the attributes were retired for responsible AI reasons, not hardware limits.
- ✗ **C. OCR to remove personal text:** OCR reads text and has no bearing on whether emotion or gender can be inferred from faces.
- ✗ **D. Limited Access application:** Limited Access gates identification and verification; it cannot bring back capabilities that have been retired.

## Key idea
Microsoft retired emotion and gender inference from the Face service; do not plan solutions that rely on them.
Q006977:
## Detection, verification and identification
- **Detection** finds faces and returns where they are. It is the first step of every other operation.
- **Verification** is **one-to-one** matching: "Do these two faces belong to the same person?" Learn's example is a banking app where a user opens an account remotely by sending a new picture together with a photo ID.
- **Identification** is **one-to-many** matching: one face is compared against a secure repository of known people to find who it is, for example granting building access to a group.
- **Grouping** splits a set of unknown faces into groups that likely belong to the same person.
Verification and identification are **Limited Access** features; liveness detection is often added so a printed photo or mask cannot fool the check.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Face grouping:** it clusters many unknown faces into likely groups, which does not answer a yes-or-no identity check.
- ✗ **B. Face identification:** it searches a whole group of known people to find who someone is; the bank already knows who the customer claims to be.
- ✓ **C. Face verification (correct):** comparing the selfie with the single passport photo is a one-to-one match, which is verification.
- ✗ **D. Face detection:** it only finds where faces are and does not decide whether two faces are the same person.

## Key idea
Verification is one-to-one (is this the same person?); identification is one-to-many (who is this?); both are Limited Access.
Q006978:
## Generating images from text
**Image-generation models** create new images from a natural-language **prompt**. They rely on the same multimodal idea as captioning (learning how visual features relate to language), but in the opposite direction: text in, image out.
## How diffusion works
Learn describes **diffusion** as the technique most modern image generators use:
- The prompt identifies a set of related **visual features** that can be combined into an image.
- Generation starts from a **random set of pixel values** (noise).
- In each iteration the model **removes noise** to create structure, then **compares** the image so far with the prompt.
- It repeats until the final image depicts the described scene. Some models apply a similar process to video.
## In Microsoft Foundry
Foundry offers the OpenAI **GPT-image** series for generation and editing (inpainting with a mask and a prompt). The older DALL-E 3 model was retired on March 4, 2026, so new solutions use a GPT-image model.
## Direction check
- Image in, sentence out: captioning.
- Image in, pixel classes out: semantic segmentation.
- Text in, new image out: image generation.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Pasting detected bounding boxes:** object detection only locates objects in existing images; diffusion does not assemble a collage of boxes from training data.
- ✗ **B. Stock photo search:** that is image retrieval; a generation model creates a new image rather than returning the closest existing photo.
- ✗ **C. Pixel classification of an existing photo:** classifying every pixel is semantic segmentation, which analyses an image that already exists instead of creating one.
- ✓ **D. Random pixels refined by removing noise (correct):** diffusion begins with noise and removes it step by step, checking the result against the prompt after each iteration until the image matches the description.

## Key idea
Diffusion generates an image by starting from random noise and removing it over many iterations, guided by the prompt, until the picture matches the description.
Q006979:
## From pages to fields
Extracting information from documents is usually a pipeline:
- **Content extraction**: OCR reads the text, and layout analysis finds paragraphs, tables, selection marks and barcodes. The output is normalized text and structure.
- **Field extraction**: a **schema** names the values you want (`SupplierName`, `InvoiceDate`, `Total`, `LineItems`) and the service returns them as **key-value pairs**, ready for an automated workflow.
Azure Content Understanding in Foundry Tools does both. It offers prebuilt analyzers (for example for invoices and procurement documents) and custom analyzers where you define your own field schema, and it can add confidence scores and grounding for each field.
## Why OCR alone is not enough
OCR tells you that the page contains the text `1,250.00`; field extraction tells you that `1,250.00` is the `Total`, whatever the layout.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Sentiment analysis:** tone scoring is a text analysis technique; it extracts no supplier, date or total from an invoice.
- ✗ **B. Image captioning:** a caption describes a picture in one sentence and does not return structured fields such as amounts and dates.
- ✓ **C. Document field extraction (correct):** a schema of named fields turns invoices in many layouts into structured key-value output that can feed the finance system directly.
- ✗ **D. Higher-resolution OCR:** better character accuracy still returns unlabelled words and lines, not which value is the total or the date, so staff would still copy values by hand.

## Key idea
OCR gives you the text; document field extraction with a schema gives you named, structured values ready for automation.
Q006980:
## Trusting extracted data
Extraction is only useful in automation if you know **how much to trust** each value and can **check** it quickly. Azure Content Understanding in Foundry Tools provides two features for this:
- **Confidence scores**: a value from 0 to 1 for each extracted field. High scores allow straight-through processing; low scores can be routed to a person. This is how you reduce manual review without blindly trusting every value.
- **Grounding**: the specific region of the content where each value was found or generated, so a reviewer can trace a value back to its origin on the page.
## Other features in the same pipeline
- **Segmentation** divides a document or video into logical parts (for example by document type, or a video into scenes).
- **Markdown output** suits search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).
Both are useful, but neither tells you how reliable a value is or where it came from.
## Example
A rule sends any claim whose `PolicyNumber` confidence is below 0.8 to review, and the reviewer's screen highlights the grounded region on the scanned form.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Markdown output:** it is a text representation for search and RAG; it gives no reliability estimate and no link between a field and its location.
- ✗ **B. Image tagging:** keywords describe what a picture shows and say nothing about the reliability or origin of extracted field values.
- ✗ **C. Segmentation:** it splits content into sections for targeted processing, which neither scores values nor shows their source.
- ✓ **D. Grounding (correct):** it shows the region of the source where each value came from, so reviewers can verify a value at a glance.
- ✓ **E. Confidence scores (correct):** a per-field reliability estimate lets the workflow send uncertain values to a human and pass confident ones straight through.

## Key idea
Use confidence scores to decide which values need human review and grounding to show reviewers where each value came from.
Q006981:
## Extracting information from video
A video combines **audio** and **visual** content over time, so extracting information from it combines several techniques and keeps **timestamps**:
- **Transcription** of the spoken words (speech to text), often with translation.
- **Scene and shot segmentation** and **key frame** detection, which split the video into meaningful parts.
- **Visual analysis** of frames: objects, on-screen text (OCR), people.
- **Summaries and descriptions** generated by multimodal models.
The output is an **index**: searchable insights linked to the moment they occur. Learn's examples include deep search ("find moments where a person spoke certain words"), creating highlight reels and accessibility.
## Services that do this
Azure Content Understanding in Foundry Tools accepts video and audio, transcribes speech, identifies key visual elements and can divide a video into scenes. Azure AI Video Indexer is a dedicated video-insights service built on Speech, Vision, Translator and Face.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Video analysis (correct):** transcription plus scene and key frame detection, all tied to timestamps, gives editors a searchable index that points to the exact moments they need.
- ✗ **B. OCR on a thumbnail:** a single image's text misses the spoken content and every scene after the first frame.
- ✗ **C. Text to speech:** it produces audio from text and extracts nothing from the videos, so there is still nothing to search.
- ✗ **D. Image classification:** one label from one frame ignores what was said and when scenes change, so editors cannot jump to moments.

## Key idea
Extracting information from video means transcribing audio and analysing frames and scenes over time, producing a timestamped, searchable index.
Q006982:
## Fields from audio
Azure Content Understanding in Foundry Tools first performs **content extraction**: for audio and video it **transcribes speech**. It then performs **field extraction** against a **schema** you define, using one of three methods per field:
- **Extract**: copy a value exactly as it appears in the content. Learn notes this method is supported for **documents only**.
- **Classify**: choose a value from a predefined set of categories, for example call sentiment `satisfied`, `neutral`, `unhappy`.
- **Generate**: produce a value with a generative model, for example a summary of the call.
Prebuilt analyzers exist for scenarios such as call center analytics, and the output is structured JSON for dashboards and automation.
## Example
Schema: `Summary` (generate), `Satisfaction` (classify: satisfied, neutral, unhappy), `Topic` (classify). Each analysed call returns these three fields ready for the dashboard.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. SSML synthesis:** SSML controls text to speech output; turning the call into more audio extracts no fields and leaves the work manual.
- ✓ **B. Transcribe, then classify and generate (correct):** speech is transcribed first, the satisfaction category comes from a fixed list (classify) and the summary is written by the model (generate), all defined by the schema.
- ✗ **C. OCR on a waveform image:** OCR reads text in images, not speech; and verbatim extraction is a documents-only method, so it cannot write a summary.
- ✗ **D. Custom speech per agent:** custom speech can improve recognition of jargon, but it is not required to fill fields, and a standard transcript feeds summaries and categories fine.

## Key idea
For audio, generative extraction transcribes first, then fills schema fields by classifying into set categories or generating values such as summaries.
Q006983:
## The six principles
Microsoft's Responsible AI Standard is built on six principles: **fairness**, **reliability and safety**, **privacy and security**, **inclusiveness**, **transparency** and **accountability**. Exam questions often describe a symptom and ask which principle it breaks, so it helps to know the core sentence behind each one.
## Fairness
AI systems should treat everyone fairly and avoid affecting similar groups of people in different ways. If two people have similar qualifications, financial circumstances or symptoms, the system should give them similar recommendations.
## Where unfairness comes from
Models learn from data that people chose and collected. If past decisions were biased, for example if fewer women were hired into engineering roles, the model can learn that pattern and repeat it, even though gender is not a valid reason to rank anyone lower.
## Example
